source: Gobet (1998) Chess players' thinking revisited
finding: Direct replication of de Groot position A with 48 Swiss players in four skill bands. Masters differed from weak players on more variables than de Groot found, but the differences were small. Total nodes, node rate and maximal depth did not differ by skill.
numbers: N=48, 12 per band (Masters mean Elo 2317, Experts 2101, Class A 1903, Class B 1699). Mean nodes 58.0, 58.3, 56.8, 33.9 (F(3,44)=1.11, ns). Max depth Masters 9.1 plies vs 8.0 pooled others (ns). Mean depth 5.0, 4.6, 3.7, 2.9 plies (F=2.9, p<.05; only Masters vs Class B reliable).
limits: Single position (easy: solvable with about 17 nodes); skill range stops at 2450; data were a secondary analysis of a controllability study (manipulation had no effect, groups pooled); audio-tape vs de Groot's note taking.
agent_relevance: Do not expect search-size differences between strong and weak models on easy items; differences show in selectivity and depth, and only on problems that need search.

source: Gobet (1998) Chess players' thinking revisited: depth slope
finding: Mean search depth rose linearly with Elo, about 0.6 ply per 200 Elo, matching Charness (1981) at 0.5 ply. This is a small, real slope, not a plateau and not a large gain.
numbers: MeanDepth = -2.638 + 0.003*Elo (p<.005). Mean depth explains about 19% of variance in move quality.
limits: Extrapolation to the top is unsafe: Campitelli & Gobet (2004) found a far steeper slope on hard positions.
agent_relevance: Depth should be an adjustable resource tied to difficulty, not a fixed constant.

source: Gobet (1998) Chess players' thinking revisited: selectivity and first phase
finding: Masters considered fewer different first moves (base moves) and spent less time on the orientation phase. Pattern recognition models predicted this selectivity; it held.
numbers: Base moves: Masters 3.2, Class A 6.5, Experts and Class B 4.8 (F(3,44)=2.94, p<.05; Masters vs Class A p<.025). 58% of Masters analysed only 1-3 base moves vs 41% of Class A analysed 9-11. First phase: Masters 1.1 min, Experts 2.3, Class A 1.6, Class B 4.2 (F=4.22, p=.01).
limits: Class A weaker than Class B on base moves, so the trend is not monotonic. Small N per cell.
agent_relevance: Strong thinking is narrow early: a short orientation, then few candidates. Our S1-S3 should cap the candidate count rather than widen it.

source: Gobet (1998) Chess players' thinking revisited: reinvestigation (progressive deepening)
finding: Returning to the same first move: stronger players did more immediate returns (the next episode re-enters the same move) and fewer delayed returns (after another move was tried). Masters produced very few delayed returns. Total returns did not differ by skill.
numbers: Total reinvestigations ns (F=0.67). Immediate returns marginal (F(3,44)=2.56, p<.07). Maximal immediate returns rises with skill (F=5.91, p<.005); maximal delayed returns falls with skill (F=3.71, p<.02). Pooled immediate returns 3.2 here vs 2.4 in de Groot; delayed 1.6 vs 1.2.
limits: Difference between 3.2 and 2.4 may be a recording artefact (audio vs notes), as the author notes. Only Masters vs Class A/B pairs were reliable.
agent_relevance: Skill shows up as depth-first persistence on one line before switching, not as more revisits. This matches the o1 underthinking result in b16 and b17: switching away too early is the weak-player pattern.

source: Gobet (1998) Chess players' thinking revisited: what predicts move quality
finding: Search variables predict chosen-move quality only partly. Elo still explained quality after search variables were removed, which the author reads as pattern recognition adding value beyond search.
numbers: Regression on time, mean depth, max returns: 35.1% of variance in move quality; Elo alone 29.2%; Elo after partialling out mean depth, max depth and nodes still 17.6% (p<.005). Move value 0 to 5 scale. Elo explains 72.3% of recall variance in a 5-second memory task (Gobet & Simon 1996c).
limits: Quality scale is coarse (one position), variance is high. Pattern recognition is inferred, not measured.
agent_relevance: Search effort alone is a weak predictor of answer quality; the quality of what is retrieved or recognised matters. Do not use depth or length as a proxy for correctness.

source: Gobet (1998) Chess players' thinking revisited: comparison with de Groot's data
finding: Pooled over skill, the 1986 Swiss sample did not differ reliably from de Groot's 1940s sample on any variable tested. The macrostructure is stable across 40 years and different recording methods. Swiss Masters looked more like de Groot's Grandmasters than his Masters.
numbers: Best move chosen by about one third of players in both samples. Swiss Masters vs de Groot Grandmasters on move quality t(15)=0.58 ns. Swiss Masters more selective than de Groot Masters (3.2 vs 4.2+ base moves; t(12)=2.20, p<.05).
limits: de Groot reported few protocols for Masters and Class players, so a formal meta-analysis was not feasible. Possible skill inflation over time confounds the comparison.
agent_relevance: The basic pattern (small trees, selective, repeated returns) is a robust description of expert thinking, so it is a safe template for a staged scaffold.

source: Campitelli & Gobet (2004) Adaptive expert decision making: skilled chess players search more and deeper
finding: On hard positions that need deep search, skill effects on depth, node count and search rate were large and linear, from class B to grandmaster. This contradicts a plateau at expert level and de Groot's no-skill-difference result on easy positions. Position difficulty is the key moderator.
numbers: N=4 (GM 2550, IM 2500, CM 2100, Class B 1750), three positions needing 52 to 70+ nodes and 23 to 35 plies. Nodes: 370, 405, 153, 88. Mean depth: 13.8, 10.5, 7.4, 2.8 plies. Max depth: 25, 23.7, 17.7, 10.5. Rate: 12.3, 13.5, 6.8, 3.2 nodes/min. Slope 2.4 plies mean depth per 200 Elo (r=.97) vs 0.5 (Charness) and 0.6 (Gobet 1998). Top players' nodes about 10x earlier studies (387.5 vs 38.6).
quote: previous research vastly underestimated experts' search potential
limits: Only four players, one per level, ages 19 to 22; positions B and C told players there was a unique solution, a change from de Groot's instruction; no simple position under think-aloud, so difficulty and instruction are confounded.
agent_relevance: Search depth must scale with problem difficulty. A fixed small tree cap (our depth 2, 3 children) is right for easy items and wrong for items that truly need search.

source: Campitelli & Gobet (2004): same players on fast decision, memory and practice tasks
finding: The same four players that searched very deep also showed the classic pattern-recognition signatures: far better at 10-second decisions, at 5-second recall of game positions, and in hours of practice. Search and recognition co-vary with skill; they are not rivals.
numbers: 10-second tasks (49 positions, about 10.4 nodes each): GM 46.9%, IM 36.9%, CM 8.2%, Class B 4.1% correct (r=.94 with Elo). Recall of game positions 83.2, 85, 54, 47%; random positions 21.7, 19, 17.7, 15.5%; shapes about 15% for all. Cumulative study hours 6890, 7904, 1872, 416.
limits: N=4, so correlations are fragile. Simple reaction time showed no skill difference, which controls for general speed.
agent_relevance: Pattern-based fast retrieval and slow search are two modes chosen by task demand. Our schema's cheap first pass plus gated deep pass mirrors this.

source: Campitelli & Gobet (2004): strategic control of search order
finding: Kotov's advice is to list candidates, finish each line, and never jump between lines. de Groot found all players, even grandmasters, return to lines (progressive deepening). In 2004, the class B and candidate players jumped between moves without a candidate list; the GM also jumped but kept an enlarged list and tried to discipline himself; the IM followed the textbook method.
numbers: N=4. GM and IM had both read Kotov. Search order differed between GM and IM at equal strength.
quote: search behaviour is not restricted to progressive deepening but can be under strategic control
limits: Qualitative, N=1 per level. No outcome comparison of disciplined vs undisciplined search.
agent_relevance: Progressive deepening is a default habit, not a law; disciplined list-then-finish search is a trainable alternative, and which is better is untested. We could test both orders on our benchmarks.

source: Chabris & Hearst (2003) as reported in Gobet's reply: speed, blindfold and grandmaster errors
finding: Same grandmasters made more blunders when thinking time was cut about six-fold or when blindfolded. This was read as support for forward search over pure pattern recognition. Gobet's reply says the size of the effect is small and equally compatible with recognition theory.
numbers: Blunders per 1000 moves: classical (about 180 s/move) 5.02, rapid (under 30 s) 6.85, blindfold 7.63; rapid vs blindfold not different. Blunder defined as 1.5 pawns worse than the engine's best. A 36.5% rise in blunders after about 6x less time. Kasparov in simultaneous matches: median 2682 Elo, interquartile range 203.5.
limits: Read through a secondary source (Gobet's rebuttal), so the primary tables are unchecked. Chi-square on non-independent moves is questionable; a few players may carry most blunders; engine threshold catches only gross errors.
agent_relevance: A six-fold compute cut costing only about 37% more blunders suggests diminishing returns from extra thinking for strong agents. Budget decisions should be tested, not assumed.

source: Gobet (2003) reply to Chabris and Hearst: what would count as evidence
finding: Search versus recognition is a poorly posed contest because they are interleaved: recognition proposes moves and evaluations recursively during search. The SEARCH model predicts depth rises as a power function of skill, and gives a mix of move sources at grandmaster level.
numbers: SEARCH model with 150,000 chunks: 15% of moves from heuristics, 23% from chunks, 62% from templates. Blunders would rise more than 36.5% if search size scaled with time and search mattered most.
limits: The model is the author's own and was fit to earlier data; a defence of the chunking line, so treat as one side.
agent_relevance: Design tests that vary the retrieval step and the search step independently (as Berliner did for computer chess), rather than asking which matters more.

source: Bilalic, McLeod & Gobet (2008) Why good thoughts block better ones: Einstellung in chess, setup and earlier results
finding: Experts who found a familiar five-move mate stopped at it and reported searching for a shorter one but never found the three-move mate. Once the familiar route was disabled, all found the short mate. First idea blocked the better one.
numbers: Performance with the familiar solution present matched players about 3 SD (600 Elo) weaker: IMs like Class A, Masters like Class B, Candidate Masters like Class C. Grandmasters did not show it on this problem but did on harder ones. Effect depends on a skill by difficulty interaction.
limits: Numbers for the first study are restated in the second paper, not read from the original. Problem set is a few mate puzzles.
agent_relevance: A second look at a problem can be anchored by the first solution. Revisiting must be forced to differ from the first attempt (see G3 and G4).

source: Bilalic, McLeod & Gobet (2008) Experiment 1: eye movements during the Einstellung effect
finding: Players stuck on the familiar solution said they were looking for a better one. Their eyes kept fixating squares of the familiar mate for the whole time. Players who faced only the one-solution problem moved their gaze gradually to the squares of the optimal mate.
numbers: Two small groups of Candidate Masters (group sizes in a table not read). Time on familiar-solution squares did not change across six time bins (F(5,20)=0.6, ns); for the control group the squares-by-time interaction was significant (F(5,20)=11.9, p<.001, partial eta2 .75). Familiar solution found in 37 s (SD 20); control found optimal in 79 s (SD 25); the stuck group needed 148 s (SD 90) once the familiar route was removed.
limits: Very small N; eye-gaze regions chosen from expert ratings; one position.
agent_relevance: What the model says it is doing during re-search can differ from what it attends to. Revisit steps need a code-checkable difference (new candidates, new features), not a self-report. This supports G2.

source: Bilalic, McLeod & Gobet (2008) Experiment 2: the set effect lingers
finding: After failing the two-solution problem, players solved the one-solution problem more slowly than fresh players, even though they knew the position. The set effect decays slowly, like priming.
numbers: Solution time about half for fresh players at every skill level (t(44)=2.16, p=.036, d=.65); skill by group interaction ns (F(2,40)=0.9). Experiment 1 gap 148 s vs 79 s was t(8)=1.67, p=.13, d=1.2.
limits: Between-group comparison across two experiments; fresh group tested later by laptop rather than the earlier setup.
agent_relevance: After an anchoring failure, simply re-running the same prompt in the same context is likely to remain biased. A restart with a fresh context (G4 independence) is the safer revisit.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large language models cannot self-correct reasoning yet
finding: Asking a model to review and revise its own answer without outside feedback did not help and often hurt. Gains reported by others came from using the true answer to decide when to stop. This is the LLM version of revisiting a candidate without new information.
numbers: GSM8K: GPT-3.5 75.9 first try, 75.1 after round 1, 74.7 after round 2; GPT-4 95.5 to 91.5 to 89.0; GPT-4-Turbo 91.5 to 88.0 to 90.0; Llama-2 62.0 to 43.5 to 36.5. CommonSenseQA GPT-3.5 75.8 to 38.1 to 41.8. With oracle labels GPT-4 GSM8K 97.5. GPT-3.5 kept its first answer 74.7% of the time on GSM8K; changes went more often from right to wrong than wrong to right.
limits: Evaluated on GSM8K, CommonSenseQA, HotpotQA with older models (2023); does not cover tasks with external checks; prompt variants tried all failed but are a small set.
agent_relevance: Direct support for G2 and G3: a revisit step must be anchored to a real check result. Without that, revisiting costs accuracy.

source: Wang et al. (2025) Thoughts are all over the place: underthinking of o1-like LLMs
finding: Reasoning models switch among lines of thought too often on hard problems, leaving promising lines early. Wrong answers use more tokens and many more switches than right ones. Over 70% of wrong answers contained at least one correct thought. This is the reverse of expert progressive deepening.
numbers: Wrong responses used on average 225% more tokens and 418% more thought switches than correct ones (QwQ-32B-Preview, DeepSeek-R1; MATH500, GPQA-Diamond, AIME2024). Over 70% of incorrect responses had a correct thought; in over 50% of those, more than 10% of thoughts were correct. R1 thought-switch tokens on AIME2024 fell from 13.8 to 5.7 with the penalty, interval from 580.1 to 941.6 tokens.
limits: Thought correctness was judged by another LLM (about 82% accuracy on checked examples); only two model families; the penalty was tuned on AIME 2022/23.
agent_relevance: A concrete candidate fix: penalise or gate switching away from a line until a depth quota or check is met. Gated deepening fits our tree limits.

source: Wang et al. (2025): thought-switching penalty (TIP) effect
finding: A decoding penalty on switch-words (such as alternatively, wait) raised accuracy without training. The gain depends on both strength and duration; too strong and too long hurts.
numbers: On the dev set (AIME 2022 and 2023) QwQ accuracy rose from 35.2% to 39.8% when duration went 300 to 600 at strength 3; at strength 20, duration above 300 reduced accuracy. Chosen setting strength 3, duration 600. Pass@k tables were partly unreadable in the extracted text, so the test-set gains are not recorded here.
limits: Needs access to decoding logits, so not usable through a chat API. Overly strong penalty hurts. Mean gains on test sets are modest.
agent_relevance: In a prompt-only scaffold the equivalent is a code-enforced rule: stay on the current line for N steps unless a check fails (G1).

source: Muennighoff et al. (2025) s1: simple test-time scaling (budget forcing)
finding: Forcing a model to keep going, by appending Wait whenever it tries to stop, makes it re-check and raised accuracy on competition math. Other filler strings gave less or nothing. Gain is small and saturates.
numbers: s1-32B AIME24: 50.0% with no extrapolation, 53.3% with two forced Wait, 56.7% with four; MATH500 93.0 flat; GPQA-Diamond 57.6 to 59.6. Forcing twice with no string: 50.0 / 90.2 / 55.1; with Alternatively: 50.0 / 92.2 / 59.6. Rejection sampling for short answers gave inverse scaling.
limits: AIME24 has 30 problems, so +3.3 points is one problem; fine-tuned model with 1,000 examples; sequential gain flattens; forcing can loop.
agent_relevance: Weak evidence that a forced second pass helps on hard items and none on easy ones. Use a second pass only on a signal (G1), and measure per benchmark at equal tokens (G7).

source: Gandhi et al. (2024) Stream of Search: learning to search in language
finding: Models trained on search traces that include mistakes and backtracking beat models trained on only the optimal path. The model learned to search, then improved further with self-improvement.
numbers: Countdown game, small transformer trained from scratch: 51.27% on held-out inputs with search traces vs 25.73% with optimal-path training. Fine-tuned models solved about 36% of previously unsolved problems. 57.1% of training trajectories reached the solution.
limits: Trained from scratch on a toy task, not a prompted general LLM; Countdown is a clean exact-check domain; cannot assume transfer to open-ended thinking.
agent_relevance: Shows the value of visible backtracking records. In a scaffold, an explicit search log (what was tried and why dropped) is the prompt-time analogue. Not training, so only partly applicable.

source: Chassy, Lahaye, Didierjean & Gobet (2023) Intuition in chess: a study with world-class players
finding: Even after only 5 seconds of viewing, skill strongly predicted how well players evaluated a position. Search-free evaluation is real and skill-sensitive. Authors argue the data do not support a fast-then-slow two-system order; recognition and search interleave.
numbers: N=63, candidate masters to world-class. 56 positions viewed 5 s, seven-level evaluation scale vs Fritz 12. Skill accounted for 44% of variance in evaluation error. No skill effect on response time (no speed-accuracy trade-off). Complex positions evaluated worse than simple; extreme (decisive) positions evaluated worse. 37 of 3528 trials excluded.
limits: Evaluation, not move choice; the engine is the reference; 5 seconds still allows some look-ahead. Authors cite Chang & Lane (2016): stronger players search more even in speed chess.
agent_relevance: Supports a cheap first pass whose quality depends on knowledge, followed by deeper search only when positions are complex. Matches a two-tier flow but not a strict serial system 1 then system 2.

source: Chassy & Gobet (2011) Measuring chess experts' single-use sequence knowledge
finding: A large archive of games shows stronger players follow known opening sequences for longer, so a good part of master strength is stored sequence knowledge, which replaces search.
numbers: 76,562 games from 2008, players 1600 to 2399 Elo; mean game length 78.73 ply, of which 16.76 ply on average were theory, about 21.3% of moves. Authors estimate masters have memorised about 100,000 opening moves.
limits: Read abstract, introduction and methods only. Archival, so players' skills are measured by Elo only; the 100,000 estimate rests on a branching-factor assumption.
agent_relevance: Some depth is bought by retrieval, not computation. A scaffold should check a library of stored solved cases before it searches.

source: Connors, Burns & Campitelli (2011) Expertise in complex decision making: the role of search in chess 70 years after de Groot
finding: A think-aloud replication of de Groot with grandmasters through Class A: stronger players search faster than weaker ones, and all of them now search much faster than players in earlier studies. Authors conclude the overall results still support de Groot's pattern-recognition account.
numbers: 6 GMs, 5 IMs, 6 Experts, 5 Class A players, two positions each (from a search summary). Further numbers not read.
limits: Abstract level only; paywalled (Cognitive Science 35(8), 1567-1579). Numbers should be fetched before use.
agent_relevance: Rate of search, not only depth, separates skill levels; speed of generating nodes is a candidate efficiency metric.

source: Van Harreveld, Wagenmakers & Van der Maas (2007) The effects of time pressure on chess skill
finding: Across online games with different time controls and world championship matches, skill differences predicted results less well as time limits tightened. The authors conclude slow processes matter at least as much for strong as for weak players. This opposes Burns (2004) and the pure recognition reading.
numbers: No figures read; only the abstract page was opened (full text paywalled).
limits: Abstract only. Rating-based, so confounded with player style at fast time controls.
agent_relevance: Counter-evidence against the idea that expertise makes extra thinking time unnecessary; budget cuts hurt strong agents too.

source: Burns (2004) The effects of speed on skilled chess performance, as cited in Campitelli & Gobet (2004)
finding: Blitz ratings and standard-play ratings share most of their variance, and he suggested proportionally more of skill rests on fast processes at higher skill.
numbers: Blitz (about 5 s/move) shares 81% of variance with standard chess ratings (about 180 s/move), as quoted.
limits: Secondary citation only; original not opened. Van Harreveld et al. (2007) found the opposite pattern on time-control sensitivity.
agent_relevance: Rival claim to track: how much of skill survives a large compute cut is an open empirical question for us too.

source: Charness (1981) Search in chess: age and skill differences, as cited in Gobet (1998) and Campitelli & Gobet (2004)
finding: Players from 1284 to 2004 Elo on four positions with a 10-minute limit: small but reliable skill effects on depth, number of moves analysed, episodes and branches; none on search rate. He proposed that depth plateaus above candidate-master level.
numbers: About 0.5 ply of mean depth per 200 Elo; 1.5 ply per 200 Elo for maximal depth (as quoted).
limits: Secondary citation; 10-minute cap may have limited depth; skill range stops at 2004. Plateau claim contradicted by Campitelli & Gobet (2004) on harder positions.
agent_relevance: Time caps shape observed depth; a token cap will do the same to a model.

source: Saariluoma (1990) as cited in Gobet (1998): inverted-U in search with skill
finding: With a 10-minute limit on tactical positions, Masters (about 2200) searched most; the IM and GM searched less, with shallower depth. Strongest players may need less search because they see the answer sooner.
numbers: Masters: 52 nodes, mean depth 5.1; IM and GM: 23 nodes, mean depth 3.6 (as quoted).
limits: Secondary citation, tactical positions only; superseded in part by harder-position data in 2004.
agent_relevance: Search amount is not monotone in skill; sometimes more skill means less search, so effort is not a quality signal.

source: Sunde, Zegners & Strittmatter (2026) PNAS study of elite chess time use, via news report
finding: Reported analysis of about 3,600 classical games by players rated 2500+ and more than 80,000 moves; a move counted as good if it matched Stockfish 17's top choice. The press summary says long thinks can signal weaker recognition and that the study does not show forcing faster play would improve moves.
numbers: As reported by a news site, not verified against the paper.
limits: Secondary news source only; cannot be cited for numbers.
agent_relevance: If confirmed, think-time is a signal of difficulty or doubt, which supports using elapsed effort as a gate input, not as a quality score.

source: Sala & Gobet (2016) Do the benefits of chess instruction transfer to academic and cognitive skills? A meta-analysis
finding: 24 studies (40 effect sizes), 2,788 chess and 2,433 control children: small to moderate gains in maths and cognitive scores, but most studies lacked an active control group; later well-controlled trials found modest or null effects.
numbers: Summary figures from a search snippet: overall d about 0.34, maths 0.38, literacy 0.25, cognition 0.33 (secondary table). Follow-up trials N=233 and N=52 showed no significant maths problem-solving or metacognition difference.
limits: Snippet only, not opened. Mainly shows weak transfer from chess practice to general thinking.
agent_relevance: Skill in a game does not carry over to general thought without domain-matched practice; do not expect chess-style search habits to transfer to other tasks by instruction alone.
